snippet.title: The Last Old-School Mafia Boss in Los Angeles
snippet.description:
The Last Don of Los Angeles: The Story of Nick "Old Man" Licata

While the Mafia in New York and Chicago chased headlines and high-profile hits, one man in Los Angeles ruled with a different code. His name was Nick Licata.

Known to the streets as "The Old Man," Licata was the last of the "Old World" Sicilian bosses. In today’s documentary, we trace his incredible journey from a marked man fleeing the Detroit Partnership to becoming the most respected figure in the Los Angeles crime family.

In this video, we explore:
-The Detroit Exile: Why the Zerilli-Tocco regime wanted Licata dead and how he escaped to California.
-The Five O’Clock Cafe: How a modest Burbank bar became the "White House" of the West Coast underworld.
-The Code of Omertà: The incredible story of Licata’s 1969 grand jury standoff where he chose a prison cell over a single word of testimony.
-The Mickey Mouse Mafia: The truth behind the L.A. family's reputation and why Licata was the only one who could keep it together.
-Nick Licata didn't believe in the flashy life of Hollywood mobsters. He believed in silence, tradition, and the long game. This is the story of the man who beat the FBI by never saying a word.

snippet.title: Mafia in Slovakia: The Unmatched Power of Róbert Lališ and His Hit Squad
snippet.description: Slovakia's most powerful mafia boss, Róbert Lališ, known as "Kýbel," created a criminal empire that operated like a well-oiled machine for nearly two decades? Lališ took control of the infamous Sýkorovci gang after the assassination of its founder, Miroslav Sýkora, and built a mafia network that resembled the notorious Italian crime families. His gang wasn't just another criminal group—it was a highly organized syndicate with a lethal hit squad and five independent factions controlling entire regions, including Bratislava and beyond. But after years of unchecked power, Lališ's world started to crumble. His loyal hitmen turned against him, and a manhunt ensued, leading to his capture in Germany in 2015. Now, with a staggering 19 murders linked to his name, he might be on the brink of freedom again. How did he build such an empire? What led to his downfall? And could this feared mafia boss really walk free? Stay tuned, and don’t forget to hit that subscribe button and turn on notifications so you won’t miss the shocking twists in this real-life mafia saga!

snippet.title: Meet The Janitor Who Ran The Chicago Mob For 40 Years...
snippet.description:
Chicago, Illinois. Nineteen seventy-eight. The Federal Building downtown has a janitor named Tony. He's been there for years. Empties trash cans. Mops floors. Cleans the bathrooms on the third floor where the FBI has their offices.
Nobody pays attention to janitors. Nobody notices them coming and going. Nobody thinks twice about what they might overhear.
Tony's real name is Anthony Accardo. And he's not really a janitor—he just works there one day a week. Volunteers for it, actually.
Because Tony Accardo runs the Chicago Outfit. And working as a janitor in the FBI's building is the perfect way to know exactly what they're investigating.
This is the story of how a mob boss became a janitor in the FBI building. How he used that position to stay ahead of law enforcement for decades. And how he ran one of the most successful criminal operations in American history while mopping floors.

In a recent interview, rapper Afroman expressed controversial views supporting the idea of racial separation, including “whites only” towns. Afroman argued that if white communities want to exist exclusively for whites, Black people should have the same right to build their own cities or communities. He emphasized that his stance is not rooted in hatred, but in a desire for peaceful coexistence amid persistent racial animosity. Afroman spoke about his plans to create a Black-friendly community away from hostility, while acknowledging the practical need to access services from broader society. He proposed mutual respect by staying out of each other’s way, suggesting that extremists on both sides deserve space to pursue happiness. The discussion also touched on attempts to form all-white towns, like the “Return to the Land” movement in Arkansas, and extended to ideas about LGBTQ+ and other groups founding their own communities. Afroman framed these separations as pragmatic compromises rather than divisive agendas.

snippet.title: Italian Michelin-Star Chef Rates 21 Italian Food Scenes From Movies And TV | Insider
snippet.description:
Chef and restaurateur Cesare Casella breaks down Italian cuisine scenes from movies and TV based on realism.

Casella discusses the accuracy of the meatballs from "The Godfather," pasta sauce and thin garlic in "Goodfellas," and capicola in "The Sopranos." He also analyzes a dish from "Lady and the Tramp" (1955), timpano from "Big Night," the tiramisu in "Superbad," and carbonara from "Master of None." He breaks down the pasta twirling technique from "Brooklyn," cannoli from "The Bear," and calzone from "Parks and Rec." Casella reviews proper pizza throwing technique from "Seinfeld," pizza-eating form in "Eat Pray Love," lasagna-making in "Garfield: A Tale of Two Kitties," mozzarella sandwiches from "Bicycle Thieves," take-out salads from "Family Guy," Italian kitchen-table dining in "Amarcord," and trenette al pesto from "Luca."

Casella has been cooking for more than 50 years and served as the head chef at the Michelin-starred restaurant Vipore in Italy. He then moved to the United States and worked at several fine-dining Italian restaurants in New York City such as Beppe and Salumeria Rosi. Today, Casella is head of the Department of Nourishment Arts at the Center for Discovery, a residential facility in upstate New York for the medically fragile. He oversees a team of chefs, nutritionists, therapists, farmers, and educators.

You can follow Cesare on Instagram here:

Part 1: https://youtu.be/dg_XpX6IYmo
--------
In a candid interview, actor and comedian Faizon Love revealed personal struggles during a recent court appearance where it was disclosed that he makes only around $13,000 per year, mainly from royalties for the film *Elf*. Love admitted to being homeless at times and currently living with a friend in California. The 56-year-old also discussed his recent 16-day jail stint, describing the stark differences between jails in California and Florida, and noting that his stay in Florida felt surprisingly comfortable.

Love appeared in court using a wheelchair due to an injury, explaining he couldn’t walk during the hearing but can walk otherwise. The jail time caused him to miss out on a movie role, further impacting his income and career opportunities. Despite the hardships, Love maintained a candid and humorous tone, emphasizing the realities many actors face behind the scenes.
